cards.title: Write every ad as one-to-one salesmanship
cards.summary: Judge ad copy by asking whether it would help a salesman close a half-sold prospect standing in front of you.
cards.use_when: Drafting or reviewing any paid ad, product page or email where the prospect has already clicked or shown interest.
steps: Assume your reader already raised their hand — the headline or creative image earned the click, so treat the following copy as a live conversation with a warm prospect rather than a broadcast to a crowd.
For each line, ask: 'Would I say this to a buyer standing in front of me right now?' If it is something you'd only say to a mass audience, rewrite it.

Do not cap length artificially by a word count — as the source argues, confining a salesman to a set number of words would be an unthinkable handicap. Let the copy run as long as it stays interesting and useful to that one person.
Do what a good salesman does with a half-sold prospect: give enough specific information to prompt action, without boasting or showing off.
End with the equivalent of the natural close the salesman would reach — a service framed offer, not 'give me your money'.
caveats: The 'no length limit' view is Claude Hopkins' position; short-form ad formats and platform character limits may still force brevity, so adapt rather than abandon the principle.
Treat this as a copy-review heuristic, not a testable claim — you still need your own measured results.

cards.title: Long copy works when it stays interesting
cards.summary: More telling produces more selling, provided the copy holds attention on something the prospect is already interested in.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product page, landing page or advertorial should be short or long-form for an interested audience.
steps: Accept Hopkins' maxim 'the more you tell, the more you sell' — some of his most successful ads reportedly ran to around 15,000 words, framed as interesting information about a product the reader already showed interest in via the headline.
Make the copy interesting, not merely long: the source's logic is that people give time to what interests them if you make it interesting.
Only extend after the headline has confirmed interest; long copy shown to someone who never opted in is wasted.
Use this as a testable hypothesis on your own store: run a longer, information-rich variant against a short variant and measure purchase conversion, not just click-through.
caveats: The 15,000-word and other Hopkins figures describe a print-era direct response context; they are examples of what worked then, not benchmarks for modern feeds.
Do not confuse 'more you tell' with padding — Hopkins frames it as story and useful information, not repetition of features.

cards.title: Frame ads around service, not buying requests
cards.summary: Ads that ask no one to buy and instead offer service convert better because buyers act to please themselves.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer framing and call to action for an ad, landing page or door-opener promotion.
steps: Assume the reader is selfish in the ordinary sense — they care nothing about your brand, interest or profit, and only seek service for themselves.
Avoid the appeal Hopkins calls unpopular: 'Buy my brand, give me the trade you give others, let me have the money.'
Build the ad around offered service: wanted information, cited advantages to users, a genuine benefit the reader gets whether or not they buy.

Model the door-to-door hairbrush case: 2,000 salespeople were sent to say 'I was sent here to give you a brush; take your choice from these samples.' The housewife, picking one brush, saw several she wanted and felt anxious to reciprocate the gift — producing the order without any direct ask.
Apply the same structure to your offer: let the prospect choose, experience or receive value first, so the purchase becomes the natural result.
caveats: Hopkins notes these seemingly altruistic ads are based on knowledge of human nature — they are designed, not accidental charity; do not mistake this for simply being nice.
The hairbrush example is historical anecdote, not a tested result for your category.

cards.title: Spend most of your copy time on the headline
cards.summary: The headline selects and opens the door for the right readers; the entire return on an ad can hinge on it.
cards.use_when: Allocating copywriting time across a headline, subhead and body for an ad, landing page or PDP above-the-fold block.
steps: Follow Hopkins: the purpose of a headline is to pick out the people you could interest, like saying 'Hey there, Bill Jones' to one person in a crowd — headlines must not be misleading.
Recognize that most readers scan headlines and only some proceed to body copy (the source cites Ogilvy's estimate that roughly 80–90% read the headline versus the body).
Invest accordingly: Hopkins says he spent far more time on headlines than on the writing itself, often hours on a single headline and discarding scores before choosing.

Ask whether the promise — the actual benefit the customer gets from your product — is stated in the headline. The source's archetype: '1,000 songs in your pocket' puts the main appeal directly in the headline.
Because return depends on attracting the right sort of readers, cut any headline that pulls the wrong audience even if it pulls volume.
caveats: The 80–90% headline-versus-body figure is attributed here to Ogilvy, not established in the source text as a measurement; treat as a heuristic.
Hopkins reports headline changes sometimes multiplying returns five- to tenfold, and Ogilvy later reportedly saw 19-to-1 differences — these are historical observations, not guaranteed lift ranges.

cards.title: Use specificity to make claims land
cards.summary: Definitive statements with real numbers carry weight; platitudes and generalities roll off and leave no impression.
cards.use_when: Rewriting generic benefit claims on ads, PDPs or landing pages into defensible, specific statements.
steps: Identify every claim of the type 'best in the world', 'lowest prices', 'high quality' — Hopkins says these are simply claiming the expected and have no impression whatsoever.
Replace each with a definitive statement carrying an actual figure or tested fact; Hopkins notes actual figures are not genuinely discounted, while specific facts carry full weight.

Study his examples: a clothing seller claimed 'my net profit is 3%' instead of 'lowest prices in America'; a razor maker advertised a '78-second shave', indicating actual test results, versus the generic 'quick shaves'.
Make sure any figure you deploy is true and verifiable for your own product — the technique derives its power from credibility, and a false specific damages it.
caveats: Hopkins' examples come from a pre-regulatory print era; modern advertising rules on comparative and substantiated claims apply, so verify every figure you publish.
Specificity multiplies the weight of an argument you already have — it cannot rescue an irrelevant or unwanted offer.

cards.title: Exploit price perception and exclusivity psychology
cards.summary: Prices and group-restricted offers shape value perception independently of the underlying product.
cards.use_when: Framing price, tiered access, membership or VIP offers in ads and on site merchandising.
steps: Use the painting example: announced without a price, most passers-by ignored it; once told it cost $750,000, people returned and a crowd formed around it — price itself created attention and perceived value.
Consider deliberately signalling premium pricing rather than hiding it, if the product's positioning supports it, since people judge things largely by price.

Apply the tribal principle: offers limited to a defined class — veterans, lodge members, executives — outperform general offers, because those entitled to a group advantage will go a long way not to lose it.
Translate into ecommerce specifics: members-only drops, founders' pricing, a named customer segment ('for working chefs') on the landing page, or early access restricted to an email list.
Recognize Hopkins' broader point: an identical offer presented in different ways can bring multiplied returns, so the framing — not just the discount — is the lever.
caveats: The $750,000 figure is Hopkins' historical illustration, not a tested conversion result for your category.
Do not fabricate exclusivity or fake a group the customer cannot plausibly belong to; the principle rests on the buyer's belief in genuine entitlement.

cards.title: Rewrite the same offer in different framings
cards.summary: An identical offer presented differently can multiply returns, so treat the framing itself as the test variable.
cards.use_when: Planning the next round of ad, landing page or email creative variants when the offer and price must stay fixed.
steps: Hold the offer constant — same product, same price, same discount — and change one framing element at a time: the headline, the group it is addressed to, the price presentation, or the degree of specificity.
Draw your variant ideas from the source's demonstrated framing levers: headline appeal, group-restricted versus general offer, price emphasis, and concise numbers instead of generalities.

Accept Hopkins' claim that, once you find a working ad, the best way to get new customers is the way you got the previous ones — repeat and iterate on what works rather than abandoning it for novelty.
Set up the comparison so you measure purchase conversion for the same audience, since different framings attract different readers and raw volume can mislead.
caveats: Keeping the same ad and re-running it versus rewriting it is a strategic call — Hopkins advocates repetition, but modern platform fatigue effects are outside his evidence.
Framing changes can pull a different audience, so compare conversion within comparable traffic, not across mismatched segments.

cards.title: Research deeply to find the keystone fact
cards.summary: Long, tedious research often yields the single fact that becomes the backbone of a winning campaign.
cards.use_when: Preparing the creative brief or angle list for a new product launch or a stalled ad account.
steps: Before writing, gather full information on the subject, as Hopkins insists an ad writer must: read widely, including technical, dry or obscure material that was never written for marketers.

Accept that you may read volumes and find few usable facts — but one fact can be the keystone of the campaign. The source cites a toothpaste writer who read volumes of scientific matter and found in one volume the idea that 'helped make millions'.
He also cites the Rolls-Royce case, where a line found in an obscure engineering document became the basis for one of the most successful campaigns of all time.
For your store, hunt in the same terrain: supplier specs, factory documentation, warranties, ingredient sheets, support tickets, review language — places competitors have not mined for ad copy.
Treat research volume as the job: the source describes campaigns preceded by very large volumes of data and months of research, with the finished ad looking simple on purpose.
caveats: The 'millions' and campaign-success outcomes are historical case examples, not reproducible promises.
The source's maxim 'genius is the art of taking pains' is Hopkins' view of effort, not a guarantee that effort alone produces a winner.

cards.title: Keep an enduring human-psychology checklist
cards.summary: Human nature is stable, so curiosity, price perception, belonging and self-interest remain reusable copy levers.
cards.use_when: Building a standing checklist or briefing template your team uses before shipping any ad or page.
steps: Adopt Hopkins' premise that human nature is perpetual — the same today as in Caesar's time — so the psychological principles you learn will never need to be unlearned.

Include curiosity on the checklist: he calls it one of the strongest human incentives and says it should be employed whenever possible, which in ecommerce terms means intriguing headlines and open loops rather than full disclosure upfront.
Include price perception: people judge things largely by price, so decide deliberately what your price signals.
Include belonging: group-limited offers beat general ones because people will work to keep an advantage tied to their group.
Include self-interest: readers act to please themselves, never to help your profit — test every draft against that filter.
Run the draft through the checklist and flag any claim that only serves the brand.
caveats: The claim that psychological principles are fixed and enduring is Hopkins' assertion; it should not be read as evidence that any specific tactic works on every platform today.
Individual execution still requires testing — the checklist generates candidates, not proven winners for your store.

cards.title: Reconcile headline impact with measured conversion
cards.summary: Headline-driven return changes are large in the source's account, but must be verified on your own traffic and metrics.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations and measurement discipline before running a headline or creative test on your store.
steps: Note the source's claims: the identical ad run with various headlines differs tremendously in returns, and a headline change is said to multiply returns five to ten times; Ogilvy is cited as having seen differences up to 19 to 1.
Treat these as historical observations from print direct response, not as forecast ranges for your account — they justify investing in headlines and testing them.
Design your test so the headline is the isolated variable: same offer, same audience, same placement and creative where possible, differing only in headline.
Measure the metric that matches the goal — purchase conversion for a sales headline, qualified click-through if the headline's job is audience selection.
Remember Hopkins' framing that headline return depends on attracting the right sort of readers, so a lower-volume headline may be the winner if it brings better-qualified buyers.
caveats: Do not present the five-to-ten-times or 19-to-1 figures as expected lifts for a client or stakeholder; they are source-cited historical anecdotes.
Small-sample tests on niche stores may need longer runs or larger creative differences to show reliable effects.

cards.title: Choose headlines that reveal interest, not conceal it
cards.summary: A headline should work like a news headline: help hurried readers pick out what interests them without misleading.
cards.use_when: Selecting among headline options for an ad, email subject line or landing page hero.
steps: Apply the source's stated purpose: to pick out the people you could interest, the way a newspaper headline lets readers choose what they wish to read.
Keep it truthful — Hopkins stresses that headlines must not be misleading, because attracting the wrong readers wastes the entire ad spend.
Account for hurry: people want to be amused or benefited, so the headline has to deliver one of those immediately.

Recognize that a profitable product may interest a reader more than anything else, but they will never know unless the headline tells them — so the headline must surface the specific interest rather than a vague tease.
Use the 'empty church' framing: you cannot educate or inspire a prospect who never clicked, so the hook must earn attention before any persuasion, teaching or product explanation begins.
caveats: The idea that you must entertain before you educate is the presenter's interpretation of Hopkins; treat it as editorial guidance, not Hopkins' own tested conclusion.
Do not let entertainment slide into misleading curiosity — Hopkins explicitly warns against headlines that conceal the interest they should reveal.

cards.title: Match copy length and detail to the interested reader
cards.summary: Once a prospect has shown interest, give them enough information to act rather than cutting to an arbitrary word count.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much detail to include on a PDP, landing page or long-form ad for a considered purchase.
steps: Separate the two audiences: the uninterested scanner who never clicks and the interested prospect who arrived by clicking the headline or image.
For the interested prospect, follow the source's instruction to consider them as prospects standing before you seeking information, and give them enough to get action.
Do not apply mass-market brevity rules — the source argues that telling a salesman to use a certain number of words with a live prospect would be an unthinkable handicap.
Include the specific facts and service-oriented detail the prospect needs (Hopkins' razor example: a definitive '78-second shave' rather than 'quick shaves').
Review whether each added paragraph helps a half-sold buyer decide; cut content that only serves the brand or repeats the headline.
caveats: Length guidance is contingent on the prospect's existing interest — long copy shown to cold traffic or before the click is a different case the source does not address.
Platform formats (short video, display, character-limited ads) constrain this approach; apply it where the medium allows depth.

input.source_name: How to Write Ads That Sell.docx
input.text:
should be answered by the salesman's standards. Advertising is multiplied salesmanship. It may appeal to thousands while the salesman will talk to one. A mediocre salesman may affect a small part of your business. Mediocre advertising affects it all. And so he continues, there's one simple and right way to answer many advertising questions. Ask yourself, would this help a salesman sell the goods? Would it help me sell if I met the buyer in person? Some tell you to be very brief that people will read but they'll read very little. Would you say that to a salesman with prospects standing before him? Would you confine him to a certain number of words? That would be an unthinkable handicap. Consider them as prospects standing before you. So it goes back to again that idea advertising the salesman salesmanship. All your ad should be like directed to one person as if that person was standing in front of you. They've expressed interest already, right? That's what your headline grabbed them or your the image that you use grabbed them. Now that you have their attention, how would you talk to them if they're just one person? Don't speak to them in mass. Consider them a mess. I love this idea.

 Consider them as pro prospects standing before you seeking information. Give them enough to get action. So this idea of like, hey, everybody says they're not going to read or they won't listen to watch a commercial, whatever the case is.
